subject: Communication
title: The Illusory Truth Effect
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Illusory Truth Effect.

hook.text: The Great Wall of China is visible from space. It isn't. But you've heard it so many times it feels true.

buildup.text: Hasher, Goldstein, and Toppino discovered that repeated statements are judged as more true — regardless of actual truth.

discovery.text: Repetition creates cognitive fluency — the brain processes familiar info more easily, and that ease feels like truth.

twist.text: The effect works even when people are told the statement is false. Repetition overrides explicit correction.

climax.text: This is why propaganda uses repetition. This is why corrections sometimes backfire.

punchline.text: Repetition doesn't make something true. It just makes it feel true.

quiz.question: What causes the illusory truth effect?

details.summary: The illusory truth effect is the tendency to believe information is true after repeated exposure, regardless of its accuracy. Your brain uses processing fluency as a shortcut: familiar statements feel true because they are easier to process. Repetition literally creates belief.
details.whyItMatters: Advertisers, politicians, and propagandists exploit this effect deliberately. Recognizing it helps you question beliefs that come from repetition rather than evidence.
takeaways: Familiarity creates processing fluency mistaken for truth
The effect works even when you know the source is unreliable

faq.question: Does the illusory truth effect work even when people know better?
faq.answer: Yes. Research shows the effect persists even when statements contradict participants' prior knowledge. Repeated exposure creates a feeling of truth that competes with factual knowledge. This is why propaganda uses endless repetition: it works even against informed audiences.

faq.question: How can you protect yourself from the illusory truth effect?
faq.answer: Ask where your sense of certainty comes from. If you believe something because it feels familiar rather than because you can cite evidence, be cautious. Diversify your information sources to avoid echo chamber repetition. Actively seek disconfirming evidence for beliefs you hold strongly.
